course_description:
The course aims to introduce students to the Bible, to the different ways it is read, and to some of the common problems associated with interpreting it. This course may not run if there are fewer than 20 enrolments.

The course introduces students to the Bible in its historical context. How did we get the Bible? In what different ways has the Bible been read across different historical and political contexts? What relevance does the Bible have today in a "post-Christian" context? Students will encounter readings of the Bible from early councils to reformers, from First Nations perspectives to Social Justice causes.

assessment_details.title: Weekly Diary Entries
assessment_details.task_description: External students are expected to complete 8/10 diary entries over the semester, to be submitted in via Turnitin in Blackboard . Entries should be 150 words (+/-10%), and demonstrate an engagement with the course material and set readings in line with the stated topic/question found on Blackboard/Library Resources page. Diary entries are due each week starting in week 2 (due week 3) for 10 weeks (including week 12, if public holiday). Students will find the readings for each diary entries on the Library Resources page (link in Blackboard) for each respective week. Diary entries are due the week after they are assigned by 2pm (e.g. week 2 diary entry is due by 2pm in week 3 on the day of the scheduled lecture). (2.5 marks each) If 5 or fewer diary entries are completed, the student will receive 0 diary entry marks. You must include with each submission the AI declaration cover sheet (see Blackboard). This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. See late submission below. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Introduction This lecture offers an introduction to the course, its assessment, and prompts students to think about the Bible as an historical and contemporary artefact of continuing relevance.

How was the Bible Written I: From Scrolls to King James This lecture introduces the complex history of how the Bible came to be written and compiled together as canon. It traces the Bible's origins from ancient Hebrew scriptures to Christian canons, including key translations, such as the Latin Vulgate and King James Version.

How was the Bible Written II: Making the Bible This lecture looks at how different Christian canons emerged, and why various Christian traditions include different books in their bibles. It explores historical impacts of the Septuagint, the Protestant Reformation, and scholarly theories like the Documentary Hypothesis.

How was the Bible Written III: Canon from Conflict This lecture examines how various conflicts, including between Jews and Romans, as well as Christian responses to heresies like Marcionism, Gnosticism, and Montanism, helped to shape the biblical canons we have today.

The Bible, Reason, Tradition and Experience in the Christian tradition This lecture explores the Bible and its role in reason, tradition and experience, drawing on the text: God: A new Biography (London: I.B. Tauris, 2018)

The Bible and Popular Culture The Bible continues as a source to fuel imagination and story-telling, from Hollywood films to politicians who rely on ideas from the Bible to secure a moral population through returning to Biblical roots.

Empire and the Bible This lecture begins a block of three that introduce historical contexts and indigenous perspectives to think through the relationships of Christianity, the Bible, and colonisation. The first spans the 15th c. Papal Bulls, which divided the world between Spanish and Portuguese for the purposes of conquest, and the 1823 American legal case Johnson vs McIntosh, which utilised the papal bulls and other documents to determine that indigenous Americans had no right to sell the lands they occupied. The legal framework developed during this period is often known as 'The Doctrine of Discovery', and was formative for the Mabo case in Australia. The lecture includes a viewing of the 2015 documentary 'The Doctrine of Discovery: Unmasking the Domination Code', by the American indigenous scholar and activist Steven Newcomb, the co-founder of the Indigenous Law Institute. The set readings interrogate the ways in which the Bible was used to justify colonisation practices.

Indian Christianity and the Bible This lecture explores the histories and interactions of the Syriac liturgy Christians of the Malabar coast (dating to around the 2nd c. CE, perhaps earlier), the Portuguese and Catholic missionaries (especially the Jesuits), the merging and splitting of these two communities, the arrival of Protestant colonisers and (eventually) Protestant missions that led to Bible translations into Asian languages and the emergence of Christian conversion movements that articulated Dalit liberation narratives.

Indigenous Australia and the Bible This lecture focuses on Australia and, specifically, Queensland. It is framed initially within the contexts of colonisation, missionary activities, the displacement (and the concomitant cultural dislocation) of peoples onto missions and government reserves. It looks at Bible translation movements within these contexts, and at indigenous peoples’ resistance, adaptation, and agency in navigating colonial contexts. Students are introduced to three case studies of indigenous Christianities that are derived from research conducted for the Queensland Atlas of Religion .

The Bible and Liberation: Queer and Black Readings This lecture explores alternative readings of the Bible from historically marginalised populations, focussing on Queer theology and Black liberation theology.

The End? Revelation, the Bible, and Climate Justice The Bible has served as a window into the past as well as into the future. This lecture will explore how the Bible resources environmentalist movements, and at times, climate change denial.
Course Summary This lecture provides a summary of the course and provides opportunities for discussion.
